key_points.point: The document argues that AI teams and business teams must co-create AI solutions to ensure they are executable and impactful, moving beyond a 'build it and they will come' mentality.
key_points.verbatim: Defining a robust value hypothesis therefore requires co-creation. Business leaders know how processes really work, what levers actually drive change, and what's realistic given current operations. AI teams understand technical possibilities, scalability challenges, and innovation.
key_points.excerpt_context: Section: Defining a robust value hypothesis therefore requires co-creation.

key_points.point: The document emphasizes that AI success is not just about technical excellence but about embedding AI into workflows and organizational processes to drive real-world performance.
key_points.verbatim: Value doesn’t emerge from technical excellence alone. It requires business teams to advocate for change and back that advocacy with tangible contributions of budget, people, and time.
key_points.excerpt_context: Section: Why the business teams need skin in the game

key_points.point: The document argues that AI initiatives often fail due to human and organizational barriers, suggesting that safety and success depend on rigorous process and people-first integration rather than just model accuracy.
key_points.verbatim: Most AI initiatives don’t fail because of flawed models but because of human and organizational barriers. Misaligned processes, resistance from employees, lack of cross-functional ownership.
key_points.excerpt_context: Section: Value-first also means process- and people-first

key_points.point: The document stresses that AI must be seamlessly embedded into workflows and that employees must trust and understand the tools, which is a form of human-in-the-loop safety and adoption assurance.
key_points.verbatim: People engagement: requires clear communication, proper training, and the right incentives to help employees trust and adopt AI-driven changes in their daily work.
key_points.excerpt_context: Section: What does this look like in practice?

key_points.point: The document highlights the 'Proof-of-Concept Trap,' where organizations fail to scale AI because they lack the necessary infrastructure and strategic planning, reflecting a skeptical view of AI's immediate enterprise-wide impact.
key_points.verbatim: Many organizations fall into the same trap. They think that if their data and AI teams “just deliver great models,” the value will automatically follow. Business teams throw requirements over the fence and expect the technology side to do the rest.
key_points.excerpt_context: Section: The myth of "just build it and they'll come"

key_points.point: The document acknowledges that AI adoption can lead to resistance and stress among employees, validating the skeptic's concern about the human cost of automation.
key_points.verbatim: Employees often worry about what AI means for their jobs. Without clear communication, fear quickly turns into resistance.

factual_claims.claim: Most AI initiatives fail due to human and organizational barriers rather than flawed technical models.
Value from AI emerges only when technical capabilities are embedded into existing business workflows and processes.

unmapped_concepts.suggested_description: The requirement that business stakeholders take active responsibility for AI outcomes by contributing budget, personnel, and process redesign. It shifts AI from a technical project to an organizational capability.
unmapped_concepts.concept: The document argues that AI value is only realized when business teams move from a spectator mindset to co-owners who actively shape, adopt, and sustain AI use cases.
unmapped_concepts.reason: This concept bridges the gap between technical development and organizational adoption, which is currently missing from the taxonomy.
unmapped_concepts.Accelerationist Interpretation: Business skin in the game is a necessary condition for scaling AI and capturing its full economic potential.
unmapped_concepts.Safetyist Interpretation: Business skin in the game ensures that human oversight and accountability are integrated into AI deployment, reducing the risk of autonomous, unmonitored failures.
unmapped_concepts.Skeptic Interpretation: Business skin in the game is a way to force business leaders to confront the real-world costs and organizational disruptions of AI, preventing them from treating it as a 'magic' technical solution.

unmapped_concepts.suggested_description: The phenomenon where organizations fund numerous low-cost, isolated AI pilots but fail to scale them due to a lack of infrastructure, integration, and strategic roadmap.
unmapped_concepts.concept: The document describes how many organizations get stuck in a cycle of delivering prototypes instead of transformation because they lack the necessary business commitment and integration.
unmapped_concepts.reason: This concept explains the gap between AI experimentation and enterprise-wide transformation, which is a key concern for skeptics of AI hype.
